proof_summary: For an arbitrary bound \(B\), apply the assumed representation to \(n=(B+6)!\); if either the resulting Sophie Germain prime or twin-prime pair were bounded by \(B\), an appropriate prime term would divide \(n\), and the identity \((6x-1)+(6y+1)=6n\) would make it divide the prime term on the other side. Primality would force those terms to be equal, whereas the factorial size bounds force a strict inequality, so both kinds of primes occur above every bound.
